asr_text: A conversation can feel uncomfortable before anyone says anything rude. Sometimes, all it takes is a short silence. In a 2011 study, 102 university students read a group conversation. After a mildly controversial comment, one group saw the conversation continue. The other group saw a brief silent moment. The silence changed how people felt. They reported more rejection and more negative feelings. They also felt less accepted, less confident, and less sure that the group agreed with them. A different study used a six-minute video of a conversation. Some viewers saw one four-second silence in the video. Most did not notice the exact pause. Even so, they reported a similar feeling of rejection and less connection than viewers who saw the conversation without the pause. But silence does not mean the same thing in every conversation. In natural 10-minute conversations, long gaps of more than two seconds were more common between friends than between strangers. For strangers, these gaps were linked with less momentary connection. For friends, they were linked with more connection. Other people who watched the conversations also rated the gaps between strangers as more awkward.
